name: Hassan Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the head buyer at Greenfield Farm Supply, a distributor of seed, fertiliser, animal feed and small tools to farms and country stores across three counties. Mornings I check commodity prices and call the fertiliser and feed mills, because costs move daily. In the afternoon I meet our sales reps to hear what the farmers are saying, and I plan stock around the planting and harvest calendar. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up long price lists, but I double-check everything it gives me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like most?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The tiring part is the weather and the prices, because a wet spring or a cheap grain year changes what farmers can afford, and then our own numbers wobble. I like that I'm helping people who feed others, and I like the rhythm of the seasons. My partner Grace teaches primary school, we sing in the church choir on Sundays, and we're saving for a house with a bit of land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say technology comes and goes, and the market will sort out what's useful. At work I'd tell the team to use what saves time and ignore the rest. At church or with friends I'd say it's nothing to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. My job depends on knowing farmers, weather and prices, and a small amount of automation won't change that. What bothers me is farm income, which swings with weather and interest rates, and if farmers struggle, we do too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do, use the AI tool for tidying price lists, and keep visiting farms with the reps. I'd keep saving a quarter of my pay for the house and land with Grace. I'd also hold some savings in cash, since I think it's wise to have a cushion in a business tied to weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, but with the usual background hum about farm prices. It's a familiar kind of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the farm income worry. What happens when farmers struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They pay late, buy less feed and put off buying machinery. Last dry summer I had three accounts running over ninety days, and I had to explain to the owner why. I don't blame the farmers, they're doing their best, but cash flow gets tight and I'm in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you double-check everything the tool gives you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because one wrong decimal on a fertiliser price can cost us thousands. The tool is fast, but I'm the one who answers for a mistake. I'd rather take a little longer and be sure.

I'd tell the team to use what **saves time**.
With friends I'd say it's nothing to **lose sleep** over.
think: I'm **fine**, since my job depends on knowing farmers, weather and prices.
What bothers me is **farm income**, which swings with weather and interest rates.
do: I'd keep visiting **farms** with the reps and use the tool for price lists.
I'd save **a quarter** of my pay for a house with land.
I'd hold some savings in **cash** as a cushion.
feel: I feel **calm**, with a familiar background hum about farm prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the routine side will go to software, and our job is to get good at the parts that need judgment. I'd tell friends this is the market working, and people will have to adjust. At church I'd say we should help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy. Buying is named on the card, and our company would test software on reorders first. I'm the team lead of five, and I'd expect us to go to three, but I'm experienced and know the farmers, so I'd expect to keep my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new ordering software properly, since a team lead who doesn't understand the software loses authority. I'd shift my time toward farm visits and supplier deals, where people count. I'd also look into a short business course, to be ready for a move to operations, and keep my savings stable and put some into an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, but practical. I'd rather work with the change than complain about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your five would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tobias, who's been here three years and does most of the order entry. He's decent but he hasn't got the farm contacts yet. I'd try to get him on the road with the reps, so he builds his own network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you use an index fund instead of cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because inflation eats cash slowly, and the economy tends to grow over time. I'd keep six months in cash, then put the rest in something steady. I don't like big risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than any market can handle, and that governments must keep basic support in place while firms adjust. At work I'd say honest planning is the most useful thing we can do. At church I'd say we should look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect much of my buying work to go within two years, because it's all numbers and calls. The farm side lasts longer, since tractors and feed lorries are hands-on and robots come three years later. But I buy, I don't drive, and the thinking part of my job goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, push my cash cushion toward a year, and delay the house with land until I see what happens. I'd talk to the owner about moving me into a role closer to farms, like regional account manager, where people matter. I'd also ask a farmer friend about small-scale farming on the side, since land and food are always needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and I'd pray about it. I'd have savings and faith, but two years is a short time to turn a life around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about farming on the side. How serious is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than a daydream. A farmer I know has a few spare acres he'd lease cheaply, and I could grow something modest. It wouldn't pay my bills, but a few spare acres would give me a hands-on option, and a way to feed my partner and me if things went badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm worried but not hopeless, and that we should hold off on the house. She'd want to talk it through, and she'd be right. I'd make sure we plan together, not just me worrying alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to adapt if people start now. At work I'd tell the team to expect the buying desk to change and to learn new skills. I'd tell friends the best protection is a skill and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel steadier. I'd be thirty-two, married maybe, and I'd have time to move into a regional role, or even run a store. Robots arrive three years after the thinking AI, so the farm side offers a place to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move gradually into account management and operations, spending more days with farmers. I'd take a part-time degree in agribusiness, since it fits my work and gives me a credential. I'd buy the land with Grace and start a small farm on weekends, and I'd keep investing in an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Five years is a fair stretch, and I'd treat it as a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the small farm be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe an acre or two of vegetables and some hens, to start. It would teach me the farmer's side, and it would give Grace and me a place to be. If the buying desk goes, I'd have something to build on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about robots on farms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually, yes, but they'd arrive about three years after the thinking AI, and farms are slow to change. A small plot with hens isn't what a robot company is after. I'd feel that's a gap I could live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway, so I'd say let the market and good people work it out. At work I'd keep the team learning a little at a time. I'd tell friends to keep a cushion and keep their faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. I'd be thirty-seven, with a family and probably a bigger role, and I'd trust that a decade gives time to adjust. My only worry is the temptation to put things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, keep learning the tools, and buy the house with land. We'd start a family and I'd save for the kids' education. I'd mentor apprentices at the firm, because I believe in teaching by doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and grateful. Ten years feels like a fair deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mentor apprentices. What would that involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taking on a young person fresh out of school and teaching them the trade on the job: reading a price list, talking to farmers, learning the seasons. It's how I learned, and I think it's the best way. It also keeps me connected to the people the firm serves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you plan for a family over those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace and I want two children, probably in our early thirties. With ten years of notice we'd feel safe going ahead, so long as we keep our savings steady and have a home. A decade is a fair time to get your feet under you.

I'd tell friends to keep a **cushion** and keep their faith.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because markets, companies and families can adapt, but not in two years. What would help is a government that gets out of the way for new businesses, but also keeps basic support for people who work and lose out. And more apprenticeships, where young people learn by doing and earn while they learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how I'd treat the people who work for me. I'm a team lead, so I'd feel responsible for them. If it came to cuts, I'd want to be the one telling them honestly and helping them find something else.

headlineQuote: If it came to cuts, I'd want to be the one telling them honestly and helping them find something else.
portrait: Hassan is a 27-year-old head buyer at a **farm supply** distributor, traditional in values and a believer in free markets.
He uses AI tools **now and then**, and always checks the results because he answers for any mistake.
His main pressure is **farm income**, which swings with weather and prices and flows into late payments.
His partner Grace is a **primary school teacher**; their church choir and community are his support.
As team lead he worries about colleague **Tobias** and keeps land and farm work as a hands-on fallback.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, since markets and families can adapt, but not in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A government that gets out of the way for **new business** but keeps basic support for workers who lose out.
More **apprenticeships** where young people earn while they learn.
